payload.stem: A $10\text{ kg}$ box rests on a horizontal conveyor belt that speeds up with a constant acceleration $0.5\text{ m/s}^2$. The box does not slip on the belt, and the coefficient of static friction between the box and the belt is $0.6$. The belt's acceleration is then changed to $4$ times its original value, and the box still does not slip. The friction force on the box is now how many times as large as it was before?

options.why: Inverts the factor, thinking a larger acceleration needs a smaller friction force.
Squares the factor, as if the friction force were proportional to the square of the acceleration.
While the box does not slip, friction is the net force: $f=ma$. With the acceleration multiplied by $4$ and the same mass, $f$ is multiplied by $4$.
Uses half of the factor, as if only part of the acceleration came from the belt.
